messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Triangular Matrix Multiplication, speed up
parts:
Hi,

optimization of my GP Stan code with replacing the matrix multiplication
by a triangular matrix multiplication, gave a great speed up, 2x and more.

I'm happy, but consequently does this not also imply that there is room
for improvement in the build-in matrix multiplication of Stan?
I suspect ever multiplication is "overloaded" and goes through autodiff.
Wouldn't in be better just to pass the multiplication to BLAS and 
add the gradient directly? And use  autodiff for everthing else, execpt
precoded functions?

  vector multiply_lower_vector(matrix A, vector e) {
    vector[rows(e)] f;


    for(i in 1:rows(e))
      f[i] = A[i, 1:i] * e[1:i];  
    return f;
  }

Andre

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Triangular Matrix Multiplication, speed up
parts:
Supporting that functionality is on our to-do list. Our
plan's to do it in a more unix-like way with smaller functions
that can be easily chained rather than these mega-functions.
The mega-functions like yours lead to combinatorial explosions
in implementations and they're both hard to doc and to test
(a big red flag in API design).

So what we'd do is break down your function into two pieces:

1. extract a triangular matrix from a vector

2. multiply the matrix by a vector

So that'd look like:

triangular_matrix(v, start, m, n) * vector(u, start, n)

or until we have a triangular matrix type,

multiply_tri(triangular_matrix(v, start, m, n),
vector(u, start, n))

I didn't understand your indexing, but the above should work.

We really do want to add sparse structures, but it'll probably
be years until we can push it all through unless we get someone
dedicating themself to the task (which involves changes in the
parser, modeling language type system, I/O, and arithmetic).

- Bob

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Triangular Matrix Multiplication, speed up
parts:
Hi Daniel,

I have N parameters with a Gaussian Process, thus I get a ragged matrix array.
What I do is to enlarge my matrix to an array with dimension (N,max(dim), max(dim))
I need to take the cholesky decomposition also, thus I get triangular matrices.

Another choice is to create those matrices dynamically. For speed reasons however
I do some precalculations of the distance matrices and then use Stans 'block'  function
to extract.
Everything work fine unless it is slow. It may be due to cache limitations of the CPU.

Bob already provided some idea which I like. I also see the 'list' data structures
in Stan on "hold". There was another guy who asked for block-diagonal matrices,
I thought, if we would add a some index functions to handle triangular, block-diagonal
matrices in a flexible multiply function then we have a solution for
flexible dimension sizes.

Andre

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Triangular Matrix Multiplication, speed up
parts:
Hi Andre,

Thanks for providing more info.

My initial thoughts:
- after hearing what you're trying to do, my guess is that the memory locality isn't the bottleneck
- you'll have to dig into the C++ to figure out what's actually taking the most time; do you want to help?
- there's plenty of places to optimize at the C++ level and we're looking for more help
- I bet it's slow not because of the execution time of one log probability call; I'm guessing that you can reparameterize your model, scale your variables, and do better statistical things to make the sampling faster rather than making the execution go faster just a little bit.

Remember, Stan has to compute gradients too. So it's not just the computation time of computing the function. It's in the gradient calculation that we're actually taking a lot of time.


Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Triangular Matrix Multiplication, speed up
parts:
On Friday, December 30, 2016 at 7:20:20 AM UTC+2, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
I think going the road with the eigenvectors/eigenvalues instead 
of the cholesky decomposition is a more promising one.

In GP literature it has been stated many times that Cholesky is computationally more stable (see, e.g., GPML book, I remember there's also a paper with more details, but I don't have now time to search it).
Eigen decomposition has been used in cases where only a small number of largest eigenvalues (and corresponding eigenvectors) are needed.
The scaling of eta and sigma noise of the GP leads to just a translation and scaling of the eigenvalues.

Which is sometimes helpful, but doesn't help with changing lengthscale.

Aki

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Triangular Matrix Multiplication, speed up
parts: Dear Aki,

I think going the road with the eigenvectors/eigenvalues instead 
of the cholesky decomposition is a more promising one. 

In GP literature it has been stated many times that Cholesky is computationally more stable (see, e.g., GPML book, I remember there's also a paper with more details, but I don't have now time to search it).
Eigen decomposition has been used in cases where only a small number of largest eigenvalues (and corresponding eigenvectors) are needed.

The eigenvalues is in O(n^3) whereas the Cholesky is in O(n^3/3), however we can calculate the eigenvalues/vectors before
and then apply eta and the sigma noise. With cholesky I find only a solution for eta, but not the sigma noise.

The scaling of eta and sigma noise of the GP leads to just a translation and scaling of the eigenvalues.
 

Which is sometimes helpful, but doesn't help with changing lengthscale.

This is a problem indeed. I hope there may be a or equivalent kernels 
to address this problem. This requires more reading and understanding myself.

https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2676-using-the-equivalent-kernel-to-understand-gaussian-process-regression.pdf

Another interesting idea is to start from the Center Matrix:

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/131140/what-exactly-is-the-procedure-to-compute-principal-components-in-kernel-pca

Andre

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Triangular Matrix Multiplication, speed up
parts:
On Friday, December 30, 2016 at 4:20:12 PM UTC+2, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
The eigenvalues is in O(n^3) whereas the Cholesky is in O(n^3/3)

GPML book gives O(n^3/6) for Cholesky, although the practical implementation usually has bigger impact than these theoretical multipliers.
It's good to remember that all these O()'s are for the number of theoretical operations. This series of blog postings http://www.ilikebigbits.com/blog/2014/4/21/the-myth-of-ram-part-i gives nice analysis why
"thinking of a memory access as O(1) is generally a bad idea, and we should instead think of them as taking O(√N) time." Relataed discussion of memory locality for Cholesky can be found, e.g., here https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07527.

Aki

>
> I think going the road with the eigenvectors/eigenvalues instead
> of the cholesky decomposition is a more promising one.
>
> In GP literature it has been stated many times that Cholesky is computationally more stable (see, e.g., GPML book, I remember there's also a paper with more details, but I don't have now time to search it).
> Eigen decomposition has been used in cases where only a small number of largest eigenvalues (and corresponding eigenvectors) are needed.
>
> The eigenvalues is in O(n^3) whereas the Cholesky is in O(n^3/3),

Pedantic interlude: O(n^3) = O(n^3/3) in the usual O() notation where
constant factors don't matter.

Pragmatic reply: In reality the constant factors are much more complicated
and have to do with things like memory locality and the availability of memory
and time-efficient derivatives. The bigger advantage of using proper triangular
multiplication isn't the multiply costs, it's the size of the autodiff expression
graph.

- Bob

parts:
> On Dec 30, 2016, at 10:45 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> On Friday, December 30, 2016 at 4:20:12 PM UTC+2, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
> The eigenvalues is in O(n^3) whereas the Cholesky is in O(n^3/3)
>
> GPML book gives O(n^3/6) for Cholesky, although the practical implementation usually has bigger impact than these theoretical multipliers.
> It's good to remember that all these O()'s are for the number of theoretical operations. This series of blog postings http://www.ilikebigbits.com/blog/2014/4/21/the-myth-of-ram-part-i gives nice analysis why
> "thinking of a memory access as O(1) is generally a bad idea, and we should instead think of them as taking O(√N) time."

Serious numerical software (like Eigen) is meticulous in its
management of memory locality. But it can't make everything memory
loca. The right way to think about it is that cache misses are very
very expensive. What you're seeing in those plots from the linked
article are crossing cache sizes. So you might want to think about
it as sqrt(n), but the real issue is more that it's flat in regions
then jumps when you exceed cache.

Then you get into memory contention issues if you're running concurrently,
so that the buses and cache sizes and cache architectures make a huge
difference in efficiency.

- Bob
